units.title: Two identical environments; switch traffic in one step
units.claim: Blue and green are identical production environments: one serves live traffic while the other is idle; you deploy to the idle one, test it, move traffic in one step, and go back with the same switch. The cost is twice the infrastructure during a release.
units.explanation: Orients the reader before the procedure.

units.title: Two identical environments
units.claim: orders-blue and orders-green must have the same instance count, instance size and configuration.

units.title: A health endpoint that checks dependencies
units.claim: GET /healthz returns 200 only when the service can reach its database and its queue.
mustPreserve: only when the service can reach its database and its queue

units.title: Migrations must be backward compatible
units.claim: Database migrations must be backward compatible so the old version keeps working on the new schema; both versions share one database and a rollback does not undo a migration.
units.explanation: The hard requirement of the whole procedure.
mustPreserve: a rollback does not undo a migration

units.title: Not backward compatible: don't use this procedure
units.claim: If any migration is not backward compatible, do not use this procedure; split it into an additive release and a later cleanup release.
units.explanation: The condition under which the procedure must not run; stays with the requirement.

units.title: Access to the load balancer's listener rules
units.claim: The service runs behind a load balancer and you need access to its listener rules, because the switch changes which target group the listener forwards to.

units.title: A per-environment 5xx error dashboard
units.claim: A dashboard or query must show the 5xx error rate per environment so green's errors can be told from blue's.

units.title: Step 1: deploy the staged build to idle green
units.claim: With blue live, deploy the new version to orders-green from the same artifact that passed staging; expected: all green instances report it and blue still serves 100% of traffic.

units.title: Step 2: run the migrations once
units.claim: Apply the release's migrations once from a single job; expected: the job exits with code 0 and blue keeps serving without new errors.
units.explanation: Second step; also a live check of backward compatibility.

units.title: Step 3: all green instances must return 200
units.claim: Poll the health endpoint on every green instance until all return 200.
units.explanation: Third step: the first decision point.

units.title: Unhealthy after 10 minutes: tear down green
units.claim: If any instance still fails health checks after 10 minutes, stop and roll back: tear down green and leave blue serving; nothing was switched, so customers are unaffected.
units.explanation: The first branch; its threshold must stay on the branch.

units.title: Step 4: smoke tests must pass
units.claim: Run the smoke-test suite against green's internal address; all must pass, and a failure stops the release like a failed health check.

units.title: Step 5: point the listener at green
units.claim: Point the listener at the green target group with the modify-listener command; expected: within about 30 seconds new requests go to green and blue gets no new connections.
units.explanation: The switch; the command stays code.

paraphrase.note: The command itself is never paraphrased.

units.title: Step 6: watch the 5xx rate for 15 minutes
units.claim: Watch green's 5xx error rate for 15 minutes after the switch; if it stays at or below 2%, continue.

units.title: Above 2%: switch back to blue
units.claim: If the error rate rises above 2% at any point in the window, switch back by running the same command with $BLUE_TG_ARN; traffic returns to blue within about 30 seconds.

units.title: A switch-back can fail in-flight requests
units.claim: A switch-back after the switch is fast, but requests in flight on green during it may fail and need a client retry.

units.title: A rollback before the switch is cheap
units.claim: A rollback before step 5 is cheap because customers never saw green.
units.explanation: Why stopping at steps 3–4 costs nothing.

units.title: Step 7: keep blue as a standby for 24 hours
units.claim: Leave blue running, unchanged, for 24 hours; it is the rollback target until then.

units.title: No next-release migrations while blue is on standby
units.claim: Do not run the next release's migrations while blue is on standby, or the standby may no longer work against the schema and switching back stops being safe.
units.explanation: Condition on the standby; stays with it.

units.title: Step 8: retire blue after 24 quiet hours
units.claim: After 24 hours without a switch-back, scale blue down; it becomes the idle environment for the next release.

units.title: Record what failed before retrying
units.claim: Whichever way you roll back, record what failed before trying again; a second attempt with the same build tends to fail the same way.

mustNotClaim.claim: Rolling back (or switching back) reverts the database migrations.
mustNotClaim.why: The source says a rollback does not undo a migration; that is why migrations must be backward compatible.

mustNotClaim.claim: Traffic can be switched before the health checks and smoke tests pass.
Any error after the switch means you must switch back.
mustNotClaim.why: The threshold is a 5xx rate above 2% within 15 minutes.

mustNotClaim.claim: A non-backward-compatible migration is acceptable because you can roll back.
mustNotClaim.why: The source says not to use the procedure at all in that case.
